handover9.text: Morning, {called}. Eight months, and you've finally stopped writing your name on your coffee cup.
Post first. Rohit Kulkarni sent sweets.

then.text: He passed every exam. The note says: 'For the doctor who said no.'

else.text: He sat his exam a week after his operation and failed one paper. He's re-sitting. The sweets are still good.

then.text: And Salim Sheikh brought Pooja in again. She drew you a picture. You have three arms in it.

else.text: Salim Sheikh came for his clinic. Walks with a stick now. He asked if you were on.
else.head: tilt

then.text: Ward 4 still has six beds. Mr. Malhotra still counts them every morning, like a man checking his pockets.

else.text: And we're down to four real beds and two 'day-care chairs'. Mr. Malhotra calls that efficiency.

handover9.text: News of my own. From today, the minor cases are yours, {called}. You operate. I watch and keep my hands in my pockets.
Also, Dr. Sethi is applying for the consultant post. Expect him to be... very visible this month.

choose.text: Then give me a case.

then.text: Careful what you ask for. Priya's paging already.

choose.text: Operating while you watch is scarier than operating alone.

then.text: Good. Fear keeps your hands slow. Slow is safe.
then.head: nod

choose.text: Sethi, a consultant? Should I be worried?

then.text: Worried, no. Awake, yes. He likes credit the way Mr. Malhotra likes beds.
Grace.
then.head: shake

then.text: What? I'm a nurse. I see everything.

handover9.text: Priya: Admissions. Kitchen accident. Her hand's wrapped in a tea towel.

deepa_arrive.text: Deepa Rawat, thirty-four. Cook at the Punjab Dhaba on Station Road. A glass bowl broke in her hand.
It's nothing. A cut. Stitch it and I'll go back. Lunch rush is at twelve and Babu can't make dal to save his life.
It went through the tea towel, {called}. And two of my gauze pads.

choose.text: Let's look properly first. A glass cut can hide more than blood.

then.text: Hide? It's a cut. ...Fine. Look. Quickly.
then.head: nod

choose.text: Sit still, and we'll have you back for the lunch rush.

then.text: Don't promise the lunch rush before you've seen the wound, {called}.

deepa_arrive.text: Your case. History first: what she can tell you that the wound can't. Then the minor theatre.

deepa_brief.text: Minor theatre's ready. Local anaesthetic, saline, the fine instruments. Glass makes me nervous.
Is she going to put me to sleep?
No. You'll be awake, and you won't feel a thing once the edges are numb. {called} is operating. I'm only watching.
Only watching. Like my mother-in-law in my kitchen.
Time-out first, Doctor. I'll read the board.

then.text: It's closed, Deepa. It took longer than it should. You'll heal, but come back in two days so we can check it.
The young doctor's hands were shaking. I saw.
then.head: down

choose.text: They were. Dr. Iyer finished it. I'm sorry it was hard.

then.text: At least you say it. Babu breaks a plate and blames the plate.

choose.text: It was a difficult wound.

then.text: It was. And next time it'll be less difficult. Say that part too.
Something pulled, in there. My finger jumped by itself.
That was a tendon. It's fine, but it was closer than I like. Bend your fingers for me... good.

else.text: That's it? Stitched? I didn't feel anything after the first needle.
There was a sliver of glass in there the size of a rice grain. It would have festered for months.

then.text: And a tetanus booster before you go. Twenty years since the last one, in a kitchen wound.

else.text: Did anybody ask about her tetanus? No? Then I'll give the booster. Kitchens, Doctor.

then.text: So. Lunch rush?
No chopping for ten days. Supervise Babu. Let him suffer.

else.text: Ten days without chopping. Babu will poison half of Station Road.

deepa_after.text: Come to the dhaba, Doctor. Dal makhani. On the house. Not on Babu's days.

morning10.text: Handover, {called}, quickly. I've been here since yesterday and my coffee has its own pulse.
Bed three, Mr. Bansal, sixty-seven. Came in at two with back pain going to his groin. Blood in his urine. Kidney stone.
Painkillers, scan when radiology wakes up. He'll pass it by lunch. Easy one.
Did you examine his belly, Kabir?
morning10.head: tilt

morning10.text: At two in the morning? He had a kidney stone at two in the morning.
{called}. Bed three. Look at him yourself. Always look.

choose.text: I'll examine him properly. Painkillers can hide a lot.

then.text: Be my guest. Hide-and-seek with a kidney stone.

choose.text: Thanks, Dr. Sethi. Go and sleep.

then.text: Finally. Someone with manners.

bansal_arrive.text: Doctor. My back. Like someone is twisting a knife, then the knife goes down into my groin.
The night doctor said a stone. Forty years of cigarettes, and I get a stone? I thought it would be my lungs.
My wife is bringing my reading glasses. And my will, she says. She's joking. I think.
Examine him, {called}. All of him, not only the part with the label.

then.text: Dr. Iyer, there's a pulsing mass above his navel. His pressure's low and his pulse is fast. It's not a stone.
A leaking aneurysm. Good. Get the vascular team, cross-match six units, and don't let him sit up.
Aneurysm. That's the bad word, isn't it? On the TV it's always the bad word.

choose.text: It's serious, Mr. Bansal. But we found it in time, and the team that fixes it is on its way.

then.text: In time. I like those two words. Tell my wife those two words.
then.head: nod

choose.text: Don't worry. It's routine.

then.text: It is not routine, {called}. He deserves to know he's having a big operation.
I heard the overhead call. An aneurysm? He was fine at two. He was... he had blood in his urine!

choose.text: A leaking aneurysm can look like a stone, Dr. Sethi. His belly told me, not his urine.

then.text: ...Right. Right. I'll take him to vascular. I know the team.
then.head: nod

choose.text: It's easy to miss at two in the morning. Can you take him to vascular?

then.text: Leave it with me. I'll handle it from here.
Notice who's pushing the trolley, {called}. Remember it.
then.head: tilt

else.text: It fits a kidney stone. Painkillers and the scan.
Doctor... the room is going grey. Is the room going grey?
else.head: down

else.text: His pressure's eighty over fifty! Dr. Iyer!
Feel here, {called}. Above the navel. Feel it push against your hand? That's his aorta, leaking.
Vascular team, now. Six units of blood. Lie him flat.
I heard the call. An aneurysm? Then the junior missed it on the morning round. Unlucky.
Somebody missed it, Kabir. Take him to vascular. We'll talk later.
A man over sixty with his first 'kidney stone' is an aneurysm until you've felt his belly. Every time.

farida_arrive.text: Mrs. Ansari, yes. Chemistry teacher, Class Ten. They'll be setting fire to the lab without me.
Tomorrow's the keyhole surgery. Tiny holes, they said. I googled it. I wish I hadn't.
Pre-op check, {called}. Ask her everything that could hurt her on the table.

then.text: Aspirin this morning. Well found. I'll tell Dr. Khan; she'll want platelets in the fridge, just in case.
then.head: nod

else.text: Oh, I took an aspirin this morning, for my headache. Does that matter? Nobody asked.
It matters. It thins the blood. Ask about medicines every time, {called}. Every single time.

farida_after.text: Doctor. Tell me honestly. Can I die tomorrow?

choose.text: Any operation carries a small risk. Yours is a common one, and we're careful. I'll be there all the way.

then.text: Small risk. Careful. All the way. Three facts. I can work with facts.
then.head: nod

choose.text: No. Nothing will go wrong. I promise.

then.text: Never promise an outcome, {called}. Promise effort. Effort is yours to give.
New piece of aorta sewn in at midnight. He's in intensive care, sitting up and asking for a cigarette.
Dr. Sethi went to theatre with him. I hear he's telling the story at lunch. Loudly.

else.text: He made it. Just. He lost a lot of blood waiting for us to feel his belly.
else.head: down

else.text: Dr. Sethi is telling everyone the morning round missed it. Never mind who admitted him as a stone.

morning11.text: Now. Mrs. Ansari's gallbladder. Keyhole. You lead, I assist, Dr. Khan keeps her asleep.
Three ports, gas, the critical view. Clip the wrong tube and her liver can't drain for the rest of her life. No pressure.

choose.text: Critical view before any clip. I know.

then.text: Then let's see if your hands know it too.

choose.text: Can we go over the tubes once more?

then.text: The one you clip runs INTO the gallbladder. The fat one carries on past it. Leave the fat one alone.

farida_consent.text: Consent form. I've read it three times. It has the word 'death' on page two.

choose.text: Let me go through it. Bleeding, infection, a leak of bile. Rarely we have to open up properly. Very rarely, an injury to the main bile duct.

then.text: Rarely and very rarely. You chose those words carefully.
then.head: tilt

then.text: Good. I teach my students that words are measurements.
then.head: nod

choose.text: It's standard. Sign at the bottom and we'll get started.

then.text: Consent is understanding, not a signature, {called}. Go through it with her.
Thank you, Doctor Iyer. I'd like the long version.
Yesterday you promised me nothing would go wrong. I'm holding you to it.

farida_consent.text: If my students ask, tell them I was brave.

farida_brief.text: She's asleep. Breathing tube in, all steady.

then.text: Thank you for the note about the aspirin. Platelets are in the fridge.
then.head: nod

farida_brief.text: Ports, camera, gas, clips, the hook. Bag for the stones. All counted.
Your lead, {called}. Time-out first. Read every line like it's lying to you.

then.text: Is it done? Why does Dr. Iyer look so tired?
then.head: tilt

choose.text: It got difficult and Dr. Iyer took over. Your gallbladder is out and you're safe.

then.text: The truth, even when it's dull. Thank you.
then.head: nod

choose.text: It went fine. Rest now.

then.text: She has a right to know who finished her operation. Tell her.
It took longer than they said. My husband counted the minutes on his phone.
It did. Some bleeding, nothing worse. Her gallbladder's out and her bile ducts are untouched.

else.text: Over already? I dreamt about Class Ten setting the lab on fire.
Textbook critical view, {called}. I kept my hands in my pockets the whole time. Nearly.
else.head: nod

then.text: One thing. You reached for the main duct. You didn't clip it, but you reached. Think about why.

farida_after_op.text: Four little plasters. My students will want to see. I won't let them.

meeting.text: Morning, everyone. One case today. Dr. Sethi.

then.text: Thank you, sir. Mr. Bansal, sixty-seven. Back pain, blood in the urine. A textbook kidney stone.
But something didn't fit. I kept him under close watch, I arranged the vascular team, and we got him to theatre in time.
Excellent. A leaking aneurysm, saved. The board will love this for the newsletter.

choose.text: That's not quite how it happened. He was admitted as a kidney stone. I examined him at ten and found the aneurysm.

then.text: Is that true, Kabir?
then.head: tilt

then.text: The junior examined him. Under my supervision. Broadly. I was... nearby.
Broadly. I see. We'll talk after, Dr. Sethi.

choose.text: Dr. Sethi, what was his blood pressure when you admitted him?

then.text: His... it was normal. Probably. I'd have to check the notes.
Then check them. Sister Grace, the admission notes for Mr. Bansal, please. With the times.
With pleasure, Doctor. Every time is written down. I made sure.

choose.text: Say nothing. It's his presentation.

then.text: Thank you. Questions? No? Lovely.

else.text: Thank you, sir. A near miss. Mr. Bansal, sixty-seven, leaking aneurysm. Sadly the morning round treated it as a kidney stone.
A pulsating mass, missed by the junior. He nearly bled to death. A lesson for us all.
Missed? We can't have that in the newsletter.

choose.text: I missed it, and I'll never miss it again. But he was admitted as a stone, and nobody examined his belly overnight.

then.text: Who admitted him, Kabir?
then.head: tilt

then.text: ...I did. At two. It looked like a stone.
then.head: down

then.text: It looked like a stone to both of you. Then it's both your lesson. We'll talk after.

choose.text: Could we look at the admission notes, with the times? I'd like to learn from the whole night.

then.text: Sensible. Sister Grace, the notes for Mr. Bansal, with the times.
Is that necessary, sir? It's a teaching case.
Then let it teach us properly.
then.head: nod

choose.text: Say nothing. You did miss it.

then.text: Lessons learnt. Thank you, everyone.

meeting.text: That's all. Back to work. The patients don't wait for meetings.

raju_arrive.text: Raju Yadav, thirty-eight. Bricklayer. Lump in his left groin since last night. It won't go back in. He's vomited three times.
Doctor, it was always there, it always went back. Last night it didn't. Now it burns. Please.
Doctor! A moment, please. Mrs. Kamala Mehra is at the desk. Her son, Mr. Suresh Mehra, is on the hospital board.
She has... heartburn. And a sore knee. She'd like to be seen. First. Now. In the side room.
Eleven minutes I've been standing here, young doctor. Eleven. My son will hear about this.

choose.text: Raju first, he's an emergency. Mrs. Mehra, I'll come to you straight after.

then.text: After a bricklayer. I see. I'll remember your name.
Doctor, please, the board...
A stuck hernia goes first, Vikram. That's not my rule. It's the bowel's.

choose.text: Priya, a heart tracing and a pain check for Mrs. Mehra right now, please. Raju first. Then I'll see her.

then.text: On it. Heartburn at seventy-one could be her heart. Tracing in five minutes.
then.head: nod

then.text: A heart tracing? For me? ...Well. At least someone takes me seriously.
Good thinking. Heartburn in a woman her age gets a tracing. Now, the hernia.
then.head: nod

choose.text: Mrs. Mehra first. It'll only take ten minutes, Raju.

then.text: Ten minutes. Okay. Okay. I can... okay.
then.head: down

then.text: {called}. Trapped bowel doesn't wait ten minutes. It doesn't wait at all.

mehra_seen.text: Finally. A private room, as it should be. My son pays for half this hospital's air conditioning.
It burns, here, after my lunch. And my knee clicks on the stairs. Forty years it's clicked.
Take all the time you need, Doctor. All the time.

choose.text: Any chest pain with walking? Sweating? Breathless?

then.text: No, no. Only after spicy food. My cook is a criminal.
It sounds like acid. An antacid, a heart tracing to be safe, and smaller meals.

choose.text: It's acid. An antacid and you'll be fine.

then.text: That's it? I waited for that?

mehra_seen.text: Well. You listened. That's more than most. Suresh will hear good things.
mehra_seen.head: nod

mehra_seen.title: Fifty minutes later
mehra_seen.text: Raju has been waiting. The lump is darker now.

then.text: Doctor... where did you go? It's gone dark. Purple. The pain is... everywhere now.
Pulse a hundred and twenty. He's vomiting green, {called}.

else.text: Doctor, please. My wife thinks I'm at the site. I can't lose this job.

raju_back.text: Quick history, then theatre. Dr. Khan will want to know one thing above all.

raju_brief.text: He's vomiting, so I'm treating him as a full stomach whatever the board says. Fast tube, pressure on his throat.

then.text: And you found out he ate at five. Thank you. That's exactly why.
then.head: nod

raju_brief.text: Mesh is open. Warm swabs ready, in case the bowel's sulking.

then.text: This waited an hour, {called}. Be ready for what we find in that sac.

else.text: We're quick. That's in his favour. Your lead.

then.text: He's in intensive care. Dr. Khan is with him. The next twenty-four hours matter.
then.head: down

then.text: We took out a short piece of dead bowel and joined the ends. He'll eat again in a few days.
The bowel was bruised. Warmth brought it back. He keeps all of it.

else.text: Pink, healthy bowel. Back where it belongs, and a mesh to keep it there.
Six weeks no bricks? The contractor will give my job away.

choose.text: I'll write a letter for your contractor. Light work in four weeks, full work in six.

then.text: A doctor's letter. He'll frame it. He's never seen one.
then.head: nod

choose.text: Lift a brick before six weeks and you'll be back on this table.

then.text: Okay. Okay. Six weeks. My wife will make sure. She's scarier than you.
Fifty minutes, {called}. That's what heartburn cost him. Remember it the next time someone important is waiting.
Two hours. But your nurse did a heart tracing in five minutes. Nobody has ever done that for me so fast.
Normal, she said. So. My heartburn waited for a bricklayer.
then.head: tilt

else.text: Two hours! Two hours in a side room with a broken television, young doctor!

mehra_waited.text: Mrs. Mehra, I'm so very sorry. Doctor, please explain.

choose.text: His bowel was trapped and dying. An hour more and he'd have lost it. Your tracing was normal, and I'm sorry you waited.

then.text: Dying. In front of me, and I was complaining about my lunch.
then.head: down

then.text: My husband was a bricklayer. Before Suresh got rich. Did you know that? No. Why would you.
You did right, young doctor. I'll tell my son so. He won't like it. Good.

choose.text: He was an emergency. You weren't.

then.text: Then I'll write to the board about manners. They're an emergency too.
Doctor... true is not the same as wise.

letters13.text: Post again. You're popular this week, {called}. Mostly.

then.text: Raju's wife came by. He's off the ventilator. She brought laddoos and cried on my desk.

else.text: Raju's contractor phoned to check the letter's real. It's on his wall now.

then.text: And Mrs. Kamala Mehra wrote to the board. About you. Nicely. Mr. Malhotra read it twice. Out loud.
And Mrs. Mehra wrote to the board. About your manners. Mr. Malhotra has the letter. He's 'concerned'.
Dr. Sethi hasn't said a word to anyone since the meeting. The ward has never been so quiet.
then.head: tilt

then.text: Dr. Rao kept the admission notes. Times and all. Dr. Sethi went in to see him yesterday. He came out pale.
then.head: tilt

letters13.text: Review at three. Seminar room. Wear the clean coat.

choose.text: What if it goes badly?

then.text: Then you'll still be a doctor at four o'clock. Go.

choose.text: I'm ready.

then.text: Good. Clean coat anyway.

review_senior.text: Sit, {called}. Eight months as a Junior Resident. Dr. Iyer.

then.text: Deepa's hand: hard going, and I finished it. But {called} told her the truth about it.

else.text: Deepa's hand: neat work, and the glass found before it festered.

then.text: Mr. Bansal: a 'kidney stone' that was a leaking aorta. Found by looking. That man is alive because of one examination.

else.text: Mr. Bansal: missed, and owned. {called} has examined every 'kidney stone' since like it's a bomb.

then.text: And a keyhole gallbladder with a textbook critical view. I kept my hands in my pockets.
then.head: nod

else.text: And a keyhole gallbladder that taught us both something. Safely.
else.head: nod

then.text: You asked one question and let the notes speak. Dr. Sethi has apologised to me. He'll apologise to you.
That's how you win a fight in a hospital, {called}. Quietly, with the facts, and nobody humiliated.
You challenged a senior in front of the department. You were right. You were also loud.
Next time, come to my office first. Being right is half of it. The other half is how.

else.text: You let a colleague take your work, or your blame, and said nothing.
Generous. And dangerous. Credit is how a hospital decides whom to trust with the next patient.

then.text: The board was very pleased that her son's mother was seen promptly.
And Raju Yadav lost fifty minutes and a loop of bowel for her heartburn.
We don't run a hospital for the board, Vikram. Neither will you, {called}. Not again.
She wrote to the board. She says you were the only one who explained anything. Most... irregular.
A stuck hernia first, and the VIP won over anyway. That's the job, done well.
then.head: nod

else.text: She wrote to the board about your manners, Doctor.
And I wrote back. A stuck hernia beats heartburn. Always. Your manners we can work on.

then.text: Eight months ago you spoke up for six beds. You've kept speaking up. That's rarer than good hands.

review_senior.text: Senior Resident, {called}. Nights in charge of the whole surgical floor. An intern of your own. And a seat at the budget meeting.

choose.text: Thank you. Both of you. Dr. Iyer, for keeping your hands in your pockets.

then.text: It was very hard. Remember that when you have an intern.
then.head: nod

choose.text: I'll be ready for the budget meeting.

then.text: Wonderful. I'll send you forty pages of spreadsheets.

choose.text: I made mistakes this year.

then.text: So did I, in my year. Some of them I still dream about. Learn from yours faster than I did.
then.head: down

review_senior.text: Senior Resident. Which means my nights get quieter and yours don't. Congratulations, Doctor.
